title: Heritage sites in Delhi: Qutb Minar, Humayun's Tomb and Red Fort
seo_title: Heritage Sites in Delhi: 3 UNESCO Sites and Historic Places
meta_description: Heritage sites in Delhi: Qutb Minar, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort (UNESCO), plus Mehrauli, Tughlaqabad, Purana Qila, Lodhi Garden and Shahjahanabad walks.
summary: Delhi has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Qutb Minar and its monuments, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort Complex. Around them lie the remains of many earlier capitals, from Lal Kot and Mehrauli to Siri, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Firozabad, Purana Qila and Shahjahanabad, plus Lodi tombs, stepwells, an Ashokan edict and the colonial capital of New Delhi.

sections.h2: Why Delhi has so many monuments
paras: Delhi sits where the Aravalli ridge meets the Yamuna, a place that controlled the route between the north-west and the Ganga plains. Ruler after ruler built a new citadel nearby, which is why historians speak of the seven (or more) cities of Delhi. The ASI protects well over a hundred monuments in the city, and many more are protected by the state.

Older layers survive too. Painted Grey Ware has been found at Purana Qila, and an Ashokan rock edict is carved on a rock near the East of Kailash area. Our guide to the [seven cities of Delhi](seven-cities-of-delhi.html) explains the sequence, and the [Delhi heritage walk guide](heritage-walk-in-delhi.html) turns it into routes.

sections.h2: Delhi's three UNESCO World Heritage Sites
paras: The Qutb Minar and its monuments (1993) include the minar begun by Qutbuddin Aibak around 1199 and completed by Iltutmish, the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, the iron pillar of about the 4th to 5th century and Alauddin Khalji's Alai Darwaza. Our programme [The Qutb complex](the-qutb-complex.html) reads the inscriptions and reused temple pillars with your group.

Humayun's Tomb (1993), built in the 1560s, was the first great garden tomb of the Mughals and a model for the Taj Mahal. Our [Humayun's Tomb](humayuns-tomb.html) walk covers the tomb, Isa Khan's tomb and the Arab Serai. The Red Fort Complex (2007), Shah Jahan's palace-fort of the 1640s, includes the Diwan-i-Am, Diwan-i-Khas and the earlier Salimgarh fort; see [Red Fort Complex](red-fort-complex.html).

sections.h2: The Sultanate cities: Mehrauli to Firozabad
paras: Mehrauli has the densest cluster of monuments in Delhi: Jamali Kamali, Balban's tomb, Rajon ki Baoli, the Hauz-i-Shamsi tank and Jahaz Mahal, Adham Khan's tomb and Zafar Mahal. Our [Mehrauli Archaeological Park](mehrauli-archaeological-park.html) walk is the best introduction. Sultan Ghari, the first Islamic tomb in India, lies to the west.

The Khaljis built Siri, the Tughlaqs built Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah and Firozabad. See [Tughlaqabad Fort](tughlaqabad-fort.html), the [Begumpur Mosque](begumpur-mosque.html), [Khirki Mosque](khirki-mosque.html) and [Firoz Shah Kotla](firoz-shah-kotla.html), where an Ashokan pillar brought from Topra stands on a stepped palace building. Hauz Khas, with its madrasa and reservoir, is covered on our [Hauz Khas](hauz-khas.html) walk.

The Lodi tombs, Bara Gumbad and Shish Gumbad stand in Lodhi Garden, and Safdarjung's tomb of the 1750s is one of the last Mughal garden tombs. Purana Qila, built by Humayun and Sher Shah, has the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque and the Sher Mandal. The Nizamuddin dargah precinct, Chausath Khamba and Ghalib's tomb make a strong walk.

Shahjahanabad, the walled city of the 1640s, keeps the Jama Masjid, Chandni Chowk, Fatehpuri Masjid, havelis and gates such as Kashmere Gate. Walks include [Jama Masjid and Shahjahanabad](jama-masjid-shahjahanabad.html), [Lodhi Garden monuments](lodhi-garden-monuments.html) and [Purana Qila](purana-qila.html).

sections.h2: Colonial and modern Delhi, and planning visits
paras: After 1911 the British built New Delhi, designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker, with Rashtrapati Bhavan, the Secretariat, India Gate and Kartavya Path (formerly Rajpath). Connaught Place, St James' Church and the Mutiny Memorial on the Ridge, along with Nicholson Cemetery, record the colonial period and 1857.

Most monuments are open daily, but check the ASI website for timings before you go. October to March is the best season. For a multi-day trip, [Delhi through seven cities](delhi-through-seven-cities.html) covers the full sequence.

faq.q: How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are in Delhi?
faq.a: Three: the Qutb Minar and its monuments (1993), Humayun's Tomb (1993) and the Red Fort Complex (2007). Each is managed by the Archaeological Survey of India.

faq.q: What are the seven cities of Delhi?
faq.a: A traditional list of Delhi's historic capitals: Lal Kot and Qila Rai Pithora, Siri, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Firozabad, Dinpanah (Purana Qila) and Shahjahanabad. Historians now count more, including New Delhi, but the seven remain a useful way to read the city.

faq.q: Which are the oldest monuments in Delhi?
faq.a: The Ashokan rock edict near East of Kailash (3rd century BCE), the iron pillar at the Qutb, of about the 4th to 5th century but brought here later, and the Qutb Minar and mosque from around 1192 to 1199 onward. Purana Qila's lower layers are older still.

faq.q: What is the best heritage walk in Delhi for first-time visitors?
faq.a: Mehrauli Archaeological Park or the Qutb complex for the Sultanate period, Humayun's Tomb with Nizamuddin for the Mughals, and Shahjahanabad for the old city. Each takes two to three hours with a guide.
Most ASI monuments open daily, from sunrise to sunset, but timings and rules change. Check the ASI website or the site's own page before you go, especially for evening visits or photography.

posts.hook: Delhi has an Ashokan edict in a residential colony.
posts.caption: Near East of Kailash, a rock outcrop of the ridge carries a minor rock edict of Ashoka, more than two thousand years old.

posts.hook: At the Qutb, look at the pillars, not just the minar.
posts.caption: The mosque's colonnades reuse temple pillars. Read their carvings and the inscription over the east gate to see how the first Sultanate mosque was built.
